content: A community should carefully evaluate these recommendations and establish its own tailored response plan before the emergence of a suicide cluster. The response to such a crisis must involve all relevant sectors of the community and should be coordinated by a designated committee. This committee will oversee the day-to-day management of the crisis and ensure that all efforts are aligned. If a response plan is to be implemented, the first step should involve contacting and preparing the groups that will play critical roles in the initial days of the response. The response must be conducted in a way that avoids glorifying the victims of suicide and minimizes sensationalism. Individuals at high risk of suicide should be identified and provided with at least one screening interview by a trained counselor. These individuals should then be referred for further counseling or other necessary services. Accurate and appropriate information should be disseminated to the media in a timely manner. Environmental factors that may increase the likelihood of additional suicides or attempts should be identified and addressed. Long-term issues related to the nature of the suicide cluster should also be tackled. Recent suicide clusters among teenagers and young adults have garnered national attention, reflecting growing public concern. However, our understanding of the causes and prevention of suicide clusters remains incomplete. A suicide cluster is defined as a group of suicides or attempts that occur closer together in time and space than would typically be expected in a given community. Statistical analyses indicate that such clusters predominantly occur among adolescents and young adults, accounting for approximately 1% to 5% of all suicides in this age group. Many experts believe that suicide clusters may arise through a process of contagion, although this hypothesis has not been formally tested. Anecdotal evidence suggests that suicides occurring later in a cluster are often influenced by earlier suicides. Additionally, ecological evidence indicates that exposure to suicide through media, such as television, may increase the risk of suicide among certain vulnerable individuals, though this effect is not consistently observed across studies. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has supported several state and local health departments in investigating and responding to apparent suicide clusters. These clusters often create a crisis atmosphere within affected communities, leading to intense concern among parents, students, school officials, and others. Community leaders are frequently tasked with simultaneously preventing the cluster from expanding and managing the existing crisis. Unfortunately, opportunities for prevention are often missed during the early stages of response as leaders seek guidance on how best to address the situation. The recommendations in this report were developed to assist community leaders in public health, mental health, education, and other fields in creating a community response plan for suicide clusters or situations that may develop into clusters. Participants in the development of these recommendations included individuals who had played key roles in responding to nine different suicide clusters. They represented various sectors, including education, medicine, local government, community mental health, crisis centers, and state public health and mental health agencies. Representatives from organizations such as the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), the Indian Health Service (IHS), the American Association of Suicidology (AAS), and the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) also contributed. These recommendations are not intended as rigid instructions for every community but rather as a conceptual framework to help community leaders develop their own response plans, tailored to the specific needs, resources, and cultural characteristics of their communities. The recommendations will be periodically revised to incorporate new knowledge in suicide prevention and lessons learned from their implementation. Certain elements of the proposed plan for preventing and containing suicide clusters differ significantly from crisis-response plans for other community emergencies. These differences are primarily due to the potentially contagious nature of suicidal behavior and the stigma and guilt often associated with suicide. However, some aspects of the plan are relevant to crisis-response plans in general. State and local health planners may consider integrating the suicide-cluster response plan into existing guidelines for managing other emergencies or mental health crises. A community should review these recommendations and develop its own response plan before a suicide cluster occurs. When a suicide cluster is occurring or seems imminent, several steps in the recommended response plan should be taken immediately. For a timely reaction to be possible, the response plan must already be developed, agreed upon, and understood by all participants at the onset of the crisis. The recommended response requires significant coordination among various sectors of the community, which can be challenging even under normal circumstances and may be even more difficult during a crisis. In the early days of an evolving suicide cluster, confusion is common, and there is often a sense of urgency to take action to prevent additional suicides. However, initial efforts are frequently uncoordinated, and community members may disagree on the best course of action. Most communities eventually develop a coordinated response plan, but opportunities for prevention are often missed in the critical first hours of the response. The response to the crisis should involve all relevant sectors of the community and be coordinated as follows: Individuals from concerned agencies—such as education, public health, mental health, local government, and suicide crisis centers—should be designated to serve on a coordinating committee. This committee will decide when the response plan should be implemented and oversee its execution. One agency should be designated as the host agency for the plan, with responsibilities including convening the coordinating committee, maintaining the response plan, and revising it periodically to reflect new knowledge and community experiences. Efforts should be made to promote and implement the proposed plan as a community endeavor. No single agency has the resources or expertise to adequately respond to an evolving suicide cluster. The concept of a host agency was developed to ensure that one person or agency takes responsibility for establishing a notification mechanism, maintaining the response plan, and convening the coordinating committee. The choice of host agency should be determined by each community, and the role may be rotated among various agencies represented on the coordinating committee. The notification mechanism by which the host agency becomes aware of a potentially evolving suicide cluster will vary by community. In small communities, a single suicide may be unusual and quickly reported to the host agency. In larger communities, where suicides are more common, a more formal system may be needed to identify unusual patterns. The response plan should be implemented under either of the following conditions: when a suicide cluster occurs in the community or when one or more traumatic deaths occur that may influence others to attempt or complete suicide. It is difficult to explicitly define a suicide cluster, as the number and closeness of cases in time and space vary depending on the community's size and baseline suicide incidence. However, when a community perceives that it is facing a suicide cluster, steps should be taken to prevent further suicides that may be influenced by the crisis atmosphere or contagion. If the response plan is to be implemented, the first step should be to contact and prepare the various groups involved. Key players should be notified of the deaths that prompted the plan's implementation, their respective responsibilities reviewed, and potential challenges addressed. Timely preparation is critical to ensure an effective response. The crisis response should avoid glorifying the suicide victims and minimize sensationalism. Community spokespersons should present an accurate picture of the deceased to students, parents, family, media, and others. Announcements of school-age suicides should be made in a manner that provides maximal support for students while minimizing hysteria. Funerals should not unnecessarily disrupt the regular school schedule. Individuals at high risk should be identified and provided with at least one screening interview by a trained counselor. These individuals should be referred for further counseling or other services as needed. Active measures to identify high-risk individuals include reaching out to relatives, close friends, and associates of the deceased, as well as past and present suicide attempters. Counseling services should also be made available to those involved in responding to the crisis.
